Well that was delightful. And a challenge. Clever idea for the theme, and then clever theme entries. I was much slower than my usual time, but I never felt just stuck (well, almost never). At first I was mystified by the theme entries. Then I figured out how the circled/uncircled letters worked … then I figured out that that answer was a clue to the other entry in that row — two Aha! moments in one puzzle.

What I liked the most was that once you grasp the theme, that gives several new ways to figure out missing letters. In addition to using crosses as usual, knowing that the circled+uncircled letters had to make a phrase was a hint. In one case I figured out from crosses what the second answer in the row had to be, and then worked backward from that to figure out the circled+uncircled letters.

Always love a Simeon puzz and this is no exception, so why are all the top comments thumbs down, "a slog," etc.? There was great cluing (royal flush...I was hoping for PALACE POOS), good fill, awkward ducks like "jailable" and "complimenters" that I enjoyed seeing almost out of pity for them as words, from the lowest CASTE on someone's word-list: unwanted and hardly used.

Anyway, a good puzzle SHALL be a slog, make your brain grumble because you're making it work harder than it wants to and so it begins interrogating you as to why you're so intent on solving it. I love that feeling, it's a challenge, and I sharply tell my brain to SUCK (it) UP and get to work. That's when it gets fun, when you command your brain to bang it out!

Trigger Warning:  sappy, navel-gazing, over-wrought, pseudo-profound, Bee Ess, geeky astronomy stuff

The east end of Wisconsin Street ends in a wooden fence, which prevents both a fall of five or six feet into Lake Superior.

It overlooks mostly water, so this time of night it is dark.  Sin black, but not silent.  The waves produce funny little water sounds.

The sky tonight is not only clear, but crystalline.  The stars blaze. 

Orion is high enough that we can clearly see both him and his trusty dog and a dazzling view of Sirius--a star not only intrinsically bright, but also close, one of our nearest neighbors (8.6 light-years).

If you look closely at the thing hanging down below Orion's belt (heh heh) it looks...weird.  Like confused, or disoriented, or something.  That's the Orion Nebula trying to lure us to visit its Horsehead Nebula and Pillars of Creation and who knows what else.

And there's the red eye of poor Taurus, besieged by Orion *and* being driven crazy by a swarm of insects, the Pleiades. 

The sky was so brilliant that even my old eyes could make out individual Pleiades stars, like my much younger eyes could.

 That hasn't happened for a while, and I sure enjoyed it tonight.

Last night was an interesting solving experience for me, to say the least, so I never got the sense of how hard the solve was. Here's why.

I started solving at 6:00, but for some reason, I was called for dinner at about 6:10, not having realized that the meal was imminent.

After finishing dinner, the wife wanted to take a walk, which took about 20-30 minutes.

Then, she decided she wanted to try a new sitcom that we'd missed the first three episodes of. She needed a few minutes to get ready, so I went back to the puzzle for a few minutes.

We put the show on, and since we were using a streaming service, there were commercials. I went back to the puzzle during each break. But breaks on streaming are shorter than on broadcast TV, so I didn't get that far.

At some point, I finally finished, and found that my solve time was almost half again what it usually was for a Sunday. But I hadn't found the puzzle that hard, and I chalked it up to stopping and starting, and the conditions I was solving under.

I eventually went back up to the desktop, where I did the first part before dinner, and found that the grid had frozen where I left it, even though I had a gold star. Repeated opening and closing the site didn't change it.

So I just filled in all the missing fill, got a new jingle, and a new time as well, less than half my original one. And that's how it will go down in the books.

But that's nothing compared to my recorded time for 6/20/23:  0:00.  Go figure!
